summary: Catawba County's only fire tower: a 1951 wooden tower, replaced in 1954 by a 72-ft steel one, unstaffed by 1969, now fenced on private land.

facts.design: 1951 wooden tower on four telephone poles, under 30 ft (9 m); 1954 steel tower, 72 ft (22 m) tall
facts.status_note: No longer a working lookout; the tower stands fenced on private land

access.note: A 2026 article says the tower is fenced off and on private property

events.note: Radio and telephone line installed in early 1953, when funds for a full-time staff were also found
A new 72-ft steel tower replaced the wooden tower
By March 1969 the tower had not been staffed for over a year and a half

evidence.supports: Vernon Otto Sipe bought most of the ridge in 1943
evidence.quote: Things began to change in 1943, when Vernon Otto Sipe purchased most of the ridge of Anderson Mountain.

evidence.supports: Sipe an orchardist native to Conover
evidence.quote: Sipe, a well-respected orchardist native to Conover

evidence.supports: one-hundred-unit development planned
evidence.quote: He envisioned a one-hundred-unit development, featuring both residential homes and commercial establishments

evidence.supports: development named Anderson Park
evidence.quote: The development, named Anderson Park after the mountain

evidence.supports: development never realized
evidence.quote: Though V.O. Sipe’s vision of the Anderson Park development was never realized

evidence.supports: Sipe lived to see a fire prevention tower built at the peak
evidence.quote: However, Sipe did live to see one aspect of his vision realized: a fire prevention tower was built at the peak of Anderson Mountain.

evidence.supports: completed in early 1951; first and only tower in Catawba County
evidence.quote: The fire tower atop Anderson Mountain, the first and only tower ever built in Catawba County, was completed in early 1951.

evidence.supports: only tower built entirely of wood in North Carolina, on four telephone poles
evidence.quote: The only tower built entirely of wood in North Carolina, it was supported by four telephone poles.

evidence.supports: less than thirty feet tall
evidence.quote: Less than thirty feet tall, it was far shorter than most fire towers in the state.

evidence.supports: no radio or telephone, limiting effectiveness
evidence.quote: The lookout tower did not yet have a radio or a telephone, limiting the effectiveness of its primary function.

evidence.supports: radio bought October 1952; tower closed for the fall season
evidence.quote: When a radio was finally purchased in October of 1952, it cost so much that the tower was forced to close down for the fall fire season.

evidence.supports: radio and telephone line installed early 1953
evidence.quote: The radio and a telephone line were finally installed in early 1953.

evidence.supports: county found funds for a full-time staff at the same time
evidence.quote: At the same time, Ledbetter and the county were able to scrounge together funds for a full-time staff.

evidence.supports: Jim Ledbetter county forester in the early 1950s
evidence.quote: Jim Ledbetter was the county forester in the early 1950s

evidence.supports: Ledbetter responsible for maintenance and staffing of the tower
evidence.quote: he was also responsible for the maintenance and staffing of the tower

evidence.supports: 1954 new steel tower replaced the wooden tower
evidence.quote: In 1954, a new steel tower was built to replace the wooden tower.

evidence.supports: 72-foot steel tower rose above the treeline
evidence.quote: The new tower, seventy-two feet tall, rose above the treeline

evidence.supports: tower responded to hundreds of fires over the next decade
evidence.quote: The tower responded to hundreds of fires over the course of the next decade.

evidence.supports: an earlier article, undated here, names Stroupe as still manning the tower
evidence.quote: Clarence ‘Smokey’ Stroupe is still manning the Anderson Mountain fire tower

evidence.supports: by 1967 modern technology threatened the tower's usefulness
evidence.quote: Yet by 1967, modern technology began to threaten the tower

evidence.supports: staffing became sparse
evidence.quote: Staffing again became sparse.

evidence.supports: not staffed for over a year and a half by March 1969
evidence.quote: By March 1969, the tower hadn’t been staffed for over a year and a half.

evidence.supports: doors and windows boarded up when no staff present
evidence.quote: had to be boarded up when no staff was present

evidence.supports: chain across Tower Road kept visitors and vandals from driving up the ridge
evidence.quote: A chain was placed across Tower Road, preventing both visitors and vandals from driving up the mountain ridge.

evidence.supports: sporadic use continued, heyday over
evidence.quote: Sporadic usage continued for some time, but the heyday of the Anderson Mountain lookout was over.

lookout tower still stands

notes_for_editor: All dated history rests on one detailed local article (James Kmosko, The Chronicle Chronicle, April 16, 2026); no second source checked the dates. A Facebook search snippet (not fetched) gave 1954 and 73 ft for the current tower, close to the article's 72 ft. The article's 2026 'lookout tower' is taken to be the 1954 steel tower; that is inferred. Record location conflict is not resolved: tnlandforms gives 35.56638, -81.08833 and the Forest Lookouts page gives 35.5567, -81.0893, about 1.1 km apart, and no source read says which point is the tower. Access treated as private per the article.
